question.text: Real-estate debt is a sizeable chunk of the private debt market per Chapter 9 primarily because:

answer.text: Banks readily fund land acquisition under working-capital lines.
Real-estate debt is explicitly excluded from SEBI (AIF) Regulations.
RBI has mandated that only debt AIFs can fund real estate.

Land acquisition cannot be financed by banks under their construction-finance or working-capital schemes, opening an opportunity for debt AIFs. Additionally, land costs in metro cities often exceed 50% of project cost and collapse of some real-estate NBFCs created a lender vacuum.

explanation.text: The Logic: The workbook states that real-estate debt forms a sizeable chunk of the private debt market because land purchase cannot be financed by banks under construction-finance or working-capital schemes for large developers, that land acquisition financing creates an opportunity for debt AIFs, that land costs in metro cities often exceed 50% of project cost, and that the collapse of some real-estate financing NBFCs opened the door for private credit funds. Option D captures all four points directly. The Trap: Option A contradicts the workbook's explicit statement about bank financing for land. Option B invents a regulatory carve-out that the workbook does not state. Option C invents an RBI mandate that the workbook does not state. Note: The real-estate debt paragraph and collateral point appear on page 212; the workbook does not prescribe a specific SPV ring-fence requirement or LTV-haircut grid.
